papers.title: WMPO: World Model-based Policy Optimization for Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.authors: Fangqi Zhu, YAN Zhengyang, Zicong Hong, Quanxin Shou, Xiao Ma, Song Guo
papers.abstract:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have shown strong potential for general-purpose robotic manipulation, but their reliance on expert demonstrations limits their ability to learn from failures and perform self-corrections. 
Reinforcement learning (RL) addresses these through self-improving interactions with the physical environment, but suffers from high sample complexity on real robots.
We introduce World-Model-based Policy Optimization (WMPO), a principled framework for on-policy VLA RL without interacting with the real environment.
In contrast to widely used latent world models, 
WMPO focuses on pixel-based predictions that align the "imagined" trajectories with the VLA features pretrained with web-scale images.
Crucially, WMPO enables the policy to perform on-policy GRPO that provides stronger performance than the often-used off-policy methods.
Extensive experiments in both simulation and real-robot settings demonstrate that WMPO (i) substantially improves sample efficiency, (ii) achieves stronger overall performance, (iii) exhibits emergent behaviors such as self-correction, and (iv) demonstrates robust generalization and lifelong learning capabilities.
papers.summary: Vision-language-action models mainly learn manipulation from expert demonstrations, so they have little chance to learn from failures or to correct themselves. Running reinforcement learning on a real robot also makes samples very expensive. WMPO no longer has the policy interact with the physical environment: it first imagines trajectories with a pixel-level world model, aligns those imaginations with features pretrained on web-scale images, and then does on-policy optimization rather than the more common off-policy updates. Because the predictions are pixels rather than more abstract latents, the imagined rollouts line up better with the visual features the model already has. In simulation and on a real robot, it uses fewer samples, shows self-correction, and can keep improving. On the real robot, the base policy, a preference-optimization baseline, and this method reach success rates of 53%, 60%, and 70%.

papers.title: CamAct: Learning Robotic Manipulation from In-the-Wild Videos via Camera Motion
papers.authors: Haoming Gu, Yunpeng Qing, Zhi Hou, Weinan Zhang
papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models benefit from large, diverse datasets for robotic manipulation, yet collecting robot demonstrations remains costly. Recent work has explored egocentric videos as a source of supervision, primarily drawing on demonstrations of human-object interaction. We show that in-the-wild videos can improve robotic manipulation even when they contain no demonstrations of object manipulation. Specifically, camera motion recovered from these videos provides an additional source of motion supervision that complements robot demonstrations. Building on this finding, we introduce CamAct, which incorporates this camera-motion supervision into VLA policies alongside robot demonstrations, extending the use of human videos for manipulation learning beyond object interactions. Experiments show that incorporating this video supervision during fine-tuning improves success rates from 96.40% to 98.10% on LIBERO and from 22.96% to 29.32% on RoboCasa 365. The resulting policy also demonstrates strong results in out-of-distribution generalization on LIBERO-Plus and real-world manipulation tasks.
papers.summary: Vision-language-action models need large, diverse manipulation data, but collecting robot demonstrations is expensive. Prior work uses egocentric human video and usually only the parts that show people interacting with objects. Even when a video contains no object-manipulation demonstration, camera motion recovered from in-the-wild footage can still give a robot policy extra motion supervision, filling in what robot demonstrations do not cover. Those clips were not filmed to train robots. CamAct fine-tunes with this camera-motion supervision together with robot demonstrations. On the already strong LIBERO suite the gain is limited; on the harder RoboCasa suite, success rises from 22.96% to 29.32%. In-the-wild video does not first have to become an object-interaction demonstration: how the camera moves can itself be a signal for learning actions.

papers.title: M$^{2}$AdaptVLA: Multimodal Memory-Augmented Vision-Language-Action Model with Predictive Test-Time Adaptation
papers.authors: Liufan Tan, Tong Wang, Yuehao Yin, Jian Chen, Yihang Yin, Ying Qu, Wenyu Li, Ruyi Gan, Hao Wang
papers.abstract: Effective robotic manipulation calls for multimodal memory and rapid adaptation to shifts in contact dynamics. However, many existing policies, which retain either visual or wrench history, may miss key cues from the other modality. Moreover, even with wrench memory, fixed policies can struggle when contact conditions shift at deployment. To this end, we introduce M$^{2}$AdaptVLA, a vision-language-action model that integrates visual and wrench memories with predictive test-time adaptation. For visual memory, the model uses test-time training (TTT) to encode observation history in fast weights. Each entry in the bounded TTT bank combines the corresponding frame's features with a readout from these weights, preserving cues that predate the oldest retained frame. For wrench memory, a context gate controls how much the action expert draws on wrench history as it jointly denoises future actions and wrenches. For predictive test-time adaptation, the auxiliary wrench prediction loss also provides online self-supervision. Using measured wrenches as targets, we update low-rank policy adapters by backpropagating only through the final denoising step. Real-world experiments show that the TTT bank outperforms visual memory baselines on progress tracking, scene recall, and demonstration following. On contact-sensitive tasks, the context gate yields higher success rates than direct injection or gated cross-attention. Predictive test-time adaptation improves robustness to shifts in contact dynamics. On eight tasks requiring visual and wrench memory, M$^{2}$AdaptVLA achieves a mean success rate of 82.71%, a 31.46% absolute gain over the strongest baseline. The project page is available at https://tlf-tlf.github.io/M2AdaptVLAPage/.
papers.summary: Dexterous manipulation needs multimodal memory and has to adapt quickly when contact conditions change. Many policies keep only a visual history, or only a force and torque history, and miss cues from the other stream; even with force memory, a fixed policy can fail when contact changes at deployment. This model combines visual and force memories and adapts predictively at test time. On the visual side, test-time training writes observation history into fast weights; on the force side, a gate decides how much the action expert should use force history, while jointly predicting future actions and forces. Measured forces can also serve as online self-supervision to update low-rank adapters. On a safe-opening task, it completes 69.7% of individual keypresses, clearly ahead of controls that keep only frames or only do test-time training, and whole-task success can reach 90%.

papers.title: Cairn: Object-Centric 3D Trajectory Priors for Steering Frozen VLAs
papers.authors: Agelos Kratimenos, Kostas Daniilidis, Evangelos Chatzipantazis
papers.abstract: Vision-language-action models (VLAs) are capable low-level controllers, but they tie where objects go to the layouts they were trained on: when objects are moved or obstacles block the way, they carry them to the wrong place or into collisions. Fine-tuning on new layouts needs robot data for each one and erodes skills the model already has. We introduce Cairn, which keeps the VLA frozen and steers it at test time along learned 3D trajectories of the object in its gripper. A small prior reads point clouds of the scene and the held object, along with its pose when grasped and the instruction, and samples SE(3) trajectories up to its release that lead it around obstacles and turn it to fit through gaps. The prior and the VLA form the two levels of a hierarchical planner in which feedback runs both ways: the VLA's intended motion chooses and reshapes the trajectories, and the chosen one guides the VLA's denoising. Its predicted actions, mapped to the held object's poses through the grasp, are pulled toward the next waypoint, while the VLA's weights stay untouched. Across 1,941 held-out LIBERO scenes with displaced objects and obstacles, Cairn raises the success rate of a frozen {\pi}0.5 from 24.5% to 95.1%, above that of a {\pi}0.5 fine-tuned on our training layouts, without hurting standard LIBERO. On the third-party LIBERO-PRO benchmark, it raises success from 27.3% to 38.0%, and from 54.4% to 81.1% on the episodes it steers. On a real Franka, with a prior trained purely in simulation, it guides the frozen DROID {\pi}0.5 around an obstacle and to a placement at the limit of the arm's reach, where it otherwise fails. All code, models and data will be made public.
papers.summary: Vision-language-action models can produce low-level actions, but where an object should go is often tied to the layouts they were trained on. If objects have been moved, or an obstacle blocks the way, the policy may still carry them to the wrong place or into a collision. Fine-tuning for new layouts needs robot data for each one and can wash out skills the model already has. Cairn keeps the original model frozen and steers it at test time along a 3D trajectory of the held object. A small prior reads point clouds of the scene and the object, the pose at the grasp, and the instruction, then samples trajectories that go around obstacles and turn through gaps. The model's intended motion helps choose and reshape those trajectories, and the chosen one pulls the actions during denoising. On a layout-shift benchmark, success rises from 27.3% to 38.0%. Direct fine-tuning cuts a high success rate on the original suite by a wide margin, while this form of steering largely keeps the original level.

papers.title: DexEngine: Scaling Human Demonstrations into Physically Executable Whole-Robot Data
papers.authors: Wongyun Yu, Honggeun Kim, Donguk Lee, Minchan Kim, Kyoung Whan Choe, Minsu Cho
papers.abstract: A growing body of recent work addresses the retargeting of human hand-object demonstrations to robotic hands. To train whole-robot policies, however, the retargeted motions must be kinematically feasible and physically executable, and be produced efficiently at scale. We present DexEngine, a simulation pipeline that turns human manipulation data into train-ready, physically executable arm-hand trajectories. DexEngine first places each clip's hand-object motion where the arms can reach it, finds an arm motion that follows the human hands, and then corrects the motion in physics simulation with residual reinforcement learning. From nine human hand-object datasets, we generate about 5,200 clips for each of four dexterous hands, augmented into 65,000 trajectories (116 h) and 325,000 episodes (578 h) in total. Even with arms attached, DexEngine tracks objects more accurately than prior floating-hand methods and runs over 10x faster than RL-based ones. Policies trained on our data far outperform those trained on the same clips without physics correction or with the arms attached after a floating-hand correction, showing that fine-tuning data need physics correction. Mid-training on our data further improves them at equal fine-tuning budget, in simulation and on a real robot.
papers.summary: To turn human hand-object demonstrations into training data for a whole robot, the retargeted motions must be kinematically feasible and physically executable, and they have to be produced at scale. DexEngine first places each hand-object clip where the arms can reach it, finds an arm motion that follows the human hands, and then corrects the motion in physics simulation with residual reinforcement learning so that it can actually be executed. Starting from nine hand-object datasets, it produces about five thousand two hundred clips for each of four dexterous hands. Even with arms attached, it tracks objects more accurately than earlier floating-hand methods and runs more than ten times as fast as reinforcement-learning-based ones. Policies trained on this data far outperform the same clips without physics correction, or with the arms attached only afterwards. Without that correction, a diffusion policy succeeds in 0% of rollouts on the easier setting, compared with 53% on the corrected data.

papers.title: X-World: Transferring Video Priors to Cross-Embodiment Robot Control
papers.authors: Chun Gu, Xiaofei Wei, Yiming Chen, Juntong Zhang, Li Zhang
papers.abstract: Language-instructed manipulation requires robust closedloop policies, yet action-labeled robot trajectories are costly and limited in coverage. Human and robot videos provide complementary spatiotemporal priors for crossembodiment control. We propose X-World, which adapts pretrained video diffusion to variable views. A Q-Former compresses hidden states into tokens for a shared flowmatching expert that predicts action chunks. Datasetspecific projections map native states and actions. We adapt the backbone on large-scale robot and human videos, freeze it for action-only pretraining of the Q-Former and action expert, then post-train on the target platform. At inference, X-World responds at 20 Hz and overlaps updates with execution via asynchronous real-time chunking. X-World performs strongly on LIBERO and under zero-shot shifts on LIBERO-Plus. On hardware, it averages 81.7% success across six bimanual tasks on the side-mounted dual-arm UR5e, one of three real-robot configurations presented.
papers.summary: Language-instructed manipulation needs closed-loop policies, but action-labeled robot trajectories are expensive and limited in coverage. Human and robot videos contain spatiotemporal priors that can transfer across embodiments. X-World adapts a pretrained video diffusion model to variable views, compresses hidden states to drive a shared action expert, and uses dataset-specific projections for native states and actions. It first adapts the backbone on large-scale robot and human videos, then freezes it to pretrain the action modules, and finally post-trains on the target platform. At inference it responds at twenty hertz and overlaps updates with execution through asynchronous chunking. It reaches 98.5% average success on LIBERO, and 81.7% average success across six bimanual tasks on a side-mounted dual-arm UR5e. Priors learned from video can be connected to control on different robots.

papers.title: RoboDemo: Reconciling Demonstration Intent and Execution Progress for Long-Horizon Manipulation
papers.authors: Xiangkai Ma, Zhihao Yuan, Linbo Zhai, Xinyi Wang, Junjie Wang, Sheng Xu, Guiliang Liu, Han Zhang, Chuyi Chen, Jifeng Gao, Wenzhong Li
papers.abstract: Long-horizon robot manipulation requires more than predicting the next action from the current observation. The policy must maintain a global procedural prior that specifies the expected progress of each subtask stage, while also tracking the realized progress produced by its interactions. To this end, we propose RoboDemo, a demonstration-augmented manipulation framework built on Dual-Cascaded Test-Time-Training. RoboDemo accepts either a task-relevant human demonstration video or a semantically compatible robot video retrieved from simulation corpus as reference, allowing us to evaluate its applicability with and without paired human demonstrations. Task semantics and physical motion information from the reference video are then transferred into persistent demonstration-intent memory. During deployment, we causally compress online observations, robot states, and executed actions into interaction-progress memory. To keep reference intent stable while interaction progress continually evolves, reference and execution video tokens independently update their respective fast-weight states. The action expert performs cascaded memory reads, first obtaining reference guidance and then refining it using realized progress, allowing the policy to adapt to execution deviations without overwriting the stored intent. RoboDemo achieves 90.7% success on Imitator Game and 73.3% success across three real-world household tasks.
papers.summary: Long-horizon manipulation cannot just predict the next action from the current observation. The policy has to keep a procedural prior for how far each stage should have progressed, and also track the progress it has actually made; if those two fall out of line, later steps go wrong. RoboDemo can take a relevant human demonstration video, or a semantically similar robot video retrieved from a simulation corpus, and write task semantics and motion into a stable memory of demonstration intent. At deployment it compresses online observations, robot state, and executed actions into a memory of execution progress. The reference and the execution each update their own fast weights, so changes on one side do not drag the other off course. On a plate-on-rack task, success stays at least 97.5% across three settings; the average success on pouring is 82.9%, compared with 66.3% for a common imitation method.

papers.title: Nav4Manip: From Navigation to Dexterous Mobile Manipulation through Co-Evolution
papers.authors: Yusen Feng, Zixi Kang, Zhijun Yin, Changxiao Liu, Tianhong Gao, Jiazhao Zhang, Jiahang Liu, Libin Liu, Zhizheng Zhang, He Wang
papers.abstract: Dexterous mobile manipulation is essential for robots to perform useful tasks in complex, unstructured environments. However, existing systems face two challenges. First, navigation remains too coarse for downstream manipulation, which often requires a precise base position and approach orientation rather than merely reaching a meter-scale goal region. Second, navigation and manipulation are commonly trained in isolation, lacking a feedback loop that enables the two capabilities to co-evolve. These limitations prevent current systems from reliably executing long-horizon dexterous mobile-manipulation tasks in real-world environments. To address them, we introduce Nav4Manip, a bidirectionally coupled co-evolution system for long-horizon dexterous mobile manipulation. It comprises two complementary architectures: Nav4Manip-N learns long-horizon navigation and refines its policy through manipulation feedback, while Nav4Manip-M trains a world-action model (WAM) for downstream dexterous manipulation. We train Nav4Manip-N in three stages: multi-task co-tuning learns navigation behavior and manipulation-aware affordance prediction; rejection sampling fine-tuning (RFT) rejects low-quality policy-generated paths and fine-tunes the model on retained trajectories; and reinforcement learning from AI feedback (RLAIF) uses counterfactual preferences to further improve navigation decisions. To support this framework, we establish the Nav-N-Manip benchmark and construct Nav4Manip-Pairs from benchmark rollouts, providing large-scale paired navigation--manipulation trajectories and affordance supervision. Extensive experiments on public vision-language navigation (VLN) benchmarks and Nav-N-Manip demonstrate state-of-the-art performance, while real-world evaluations show that Nav4Manip completes diverse dexterous mobile-manipulation tasks. Project website: https://nav4manip.github.io/.
papers.summary: Dexterous mobile manipulation in complex environments often fails in two places. Navigation is usually too coarse: manipulation needs a precise base pose and approach heading, not merely arrival in a meter-scale region. Navigation and manipulation are also often trained in isolation, with no feedback loop that lets the two improve together. Nav4Manip couples them so they co-evolve: one side learns long-horizon navigation and refines the policy from whether manipulation succeeds, and the other trains a world-action model for the dexterous skill that follows. Navigation is no longer just about reaching a region; it has to hand over an endpoint the manipulator can use. Under instruction following, end-to-end success reaches 56.31%. Once the approach pose that manipulation needs is part of the navigation objective, the two sides can help each other on long-horizon tasks, instead of being trained apart.

papers.title: Entangle: Scaling Human-Video In-Context World-Action Models across Unseen Tasks and Contexts
papers.authors: Chendong Xiang, Chengwen Zhang, Ruowen Zhao, Zeyuan Wang, Shuhe Huang
papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) enables foundation models to perform unseen tasks from context without parameter updates. In robotic manipulation, a human video provides the context that specifies how a task should be performed. However, scaling human-video ICL on world-action models (WAMs) faces two challenges: task-level human-robot pairs are not temporally aligned with robot actions, and standard action losses allow policies to rely on initial-scene or task-identity shortcuts rather than tracking the context. We present Entangle, an in-context world-action model that maps a single human video and current robot observations to future visual states and executable actions. To scale temporally aligned training data, we convert recorded robot videos into matched human contexts via video-to-video generation, supplemented by real paired recordings. For model training, we combine variable-length video windows with an intra-task contrastive objective that distinguishes the paired action trajectory from other executions of the same task, preventing task-identity shortcuts. Without task-specific fine-tuning, Entangle improves steadily as aligned training data scales, reaching an average score of 83.5/100 across six unseen tasks on an Astribot S1 robot, and achieves a 69.5% average success rate on seven unseen RoboTwin tasks, outperforming Zero-WAM by 22.6 percentage points. Under Context-OOD, although trained only on scene-aligned pairs, Entangle transfers context-specified behaviors across rearranged layouts and substituted tools. Project page at https://entangle-robotics.github.io/
papers.summary: In-context learning lets a foundation model do unseen tasks from context without changing its parameters. In robot manipulation, a human video can serve as that context and show how a task should be done. Scaling this to world-action models still hits two problems: human and robot task pairs are not temporally aligned, and an ordinary action loss lets the policy take shortcuts from the initial scene or the task identity. Entangle maps a single human video and the robot's current observations to future visual states and executable actions. It turns recorded robot videos into matched human contexts with video generation, and uses an intra-task contrastive objective so the policy cannot rely on task identity alone. Without task-specific fine-tuning, it reaches an average score of 83.5 out of 100 on six unseen tasks on a real robot, and a 69.5% average success rate on seven unseen simulation tasks, 22.6 percentage points above a comparable baseline.

papers.title: Lazy gas, hot gas, and a thousand robots
papers.abstract: Viewing multirobot motion planning as an optimal-transport problem and using a Schrödinger bridge to approximate solutions enables near-optimal routing at fulfillment-center scale.
papers.summary: A warehouse floor often has thousands of robots moving at once, and they must avoid collisions while getting inventory where it needs to go. Multi-agent pathfinding is hard in general, and exact solvers struggle to keep up with real-time dispatch once the fleet grows. Amazon Robotics treats the planning problem as optimal transport: robots are modeled as a lazy, cold gas whose particles spend only the minimum effort to reach their destinations, which yields optimal, minimum-energy paths, though the computation can still be slow. Modeling the fleet as a hot gas that jitters along the way, through an entropic relaxation, is much faster and only slightly off the optimum. On a one-hundred-fifty by one-hundred-fifty grid with one thousand one hundred twenty-five robots, the hot-gas scheme returns a solution in about 67 seconds, within 6.5% of optimal. At fulfillment-center scale, a fast plan that is close enough is often more useful than waiting for an exact one.

scenario: Today's embodied papers include world-model policy optimization, so a vision-language-action model can learn to correct itself from imagined failures, and methods that take camera motion from in-the-wild videos that never show object manipulation. Others combine visual and force memory so a policy can adapt when contact changes, or steer a frozen action model along a 3D object trajectory so fine-tuning does not wash out old skills. On the data side, one pipeline turns human demonstrations into physically executable whole-robot trajectories, and another attaches video priors to control on a different body. Long-horizon tasks have to keep both demonstration intent and actual execution progress, and mobile manipulation needs navigation and dexterous skill to co-evolve. Other work uses a single human video as context, or treats pathfinding for thousands of warehouse robots as optimal transport of a gas.
